whyCorrect: The passage says the water system, not the temples, is what let a city stand where no rain falls for six months, so the advantage Angkor held is the stored and released water itself. The final sentence gives the condition under which that system fails: the channels silt up faster than they can be cleared. The blank therefore has to name the loss of the advantage, and evaporated names that disappearance in the same terms as the water it depended on.

whyWrong.B: Hardened would mean the advantage became fixed or more durable, the opposite of what silted-up channels produce.
whyWrong.C: Multiplied says the advantage grew, but the clause describes the system breaking down, so the direction is reversed.
whyWrong.D: Recurred means happened again; nothing in the text describes the advantage being lost and then returning.

tips: When the blank follows a clause beginning Once something failed, the word has to move in the direction of loss.

whyCorrect: The sentence is built as treat the number as _____ rather than decisive, so the blank has to contrast with decisive while still leaving knot count worth quoting. The examples that follow explain the contrast: fine wool badly dyed, or a design copied by someone who did not understand it, ruins a carpet at any knot density. So for weavers the count is where judgement starts and other evidence can override it, which is what preliminary names.

whyWrong.A: Conclusive is a synonym for decisive, so it destroys the contrast the phrase rather than decisive sets up.
whyWrong.B: Arbitrary is too strong: it would mean the count is assigned without reason, but the passage grants that a denser rug really does fetch more.
whyWrong.C: Fraudulent accuses the dealers of deceit, while the weavers' objection is that the number is incomplete, not dishonest.

whyCorrect: The colon means the rest of the sentence is evidence for the blank, and that evidence is all about disorder: blocks cut off-square on purpose, stripes out of alignment, a pattern abandoned halfway across. Notice the negation, though, that nothing about the results is _____, so the blank names the quality the quilts lack rather than the quality they have. Strict regularity is that quality, and the last sentence, contrasting these quilts with the neat symmetry museums once collected, confirms it.

whyWrong.A: Durable is never at issue; every detail given concerns arrangement and alignment, not how long a quilt lasts.
whyWrong.C: Improvised describes what these quilts are, so placing it after Nothing about the results is reverses the sentence's meaning.
whyWrong.D: Colour is never mentioned, and the evidence after the colon is entirely about pattern and alignment.

commonMistakes: Reading past the negation and picking the word that describes the quilts instead of the word they contradict.

whyCorrect: The colon introduces the evidence for the blank: several hundred thousand crabs bled every year, and coastal counts falling for a decade. That is a supply being drawn on faster than it can replace itself, which is what strained means. The first sentence supplies the pressure, since every injectable drug licensed in the country depends on this one source.

whyWrong.A: Synthetic contradicts the passage, whose whole point is that the test still uses blood from live animals.
whyWrong.B: Seasonal would describe a within-year cycle, but the evidence given is a decade-long decline.
whyWrong.D: Secure is the opposite of what falling counts and rising demand show.

whyCorrect: The last sentence tells you directly what the word does not mean here: historians praising the economy of this work are not talking about what it cost to build. What the paragraph does describe is a rule that nothing unnecessary to use should be made, and then unbanded drawers, pegged rather than carved chairs, and cupboards with no ornament beyond their own joints. Economy in that context means holding back to the minimum means the object requires.

whyWrong.A: Resistance to wear is about durability, but every detail listed concerns ornament left off, not hard use.
whyWrong.B: The final sentence rules out the money sense explicitly.
whyWrong.D: Speed of production is never claimed; pegging and built-in cupboards are presented as decisions about form, not shortcuts.

whyCorrect: Track the shape of the paragraph rather than any one fact in it. Albers came to paint, was sent to weaving because that is where women were sent, stayed, treated the loom as constraints to work against, published on cloth as a subject, and became the first weaver given a solo show at the Museum of Modern Art. That arc from an assignment she did not choose to the achievement it produced is the point the whole text is organised around.

whyWrong.A: The text says women were directed to weaving, which is a claim about how the school treated women, not about hostility toward painting as a discipline.
whyWrong.B: Cellophane and horsehair appear in a single clause as unusual materials; no technical comparison between them is made.
whyWrong.C: Only one exhibition, in 1949, is mentioned, and it is the endpoint of her story rather than the start of a list.

whyCorrect: Look at what sits on either side of the underlined sentence. Before it is what Anning did: found and prepared the first complete ichthyosaur to reach London and supplied dealers and professors for thirty years. After it is how she was treated: barred from the Geological Society, her labels corrected only long after her death. The underlined sentence is the hinge that first states the mismatch between contribution and credit which the rest of the paragraph then documents.

whyWrong.A: No technique is named; preparation is mentioned in the previous sentence, while this one is about whose name went on the papers.
whyWrong.B: The accuracy of the identifications is never questioned, only the attribution of the work.
whyWrong.C: The text mentions that the Society did not accept women but says nothing about why it was founded.

whyCorrect: The passage states a fact and then explains it. The fact is that both cicada intervals, thirteen and seventeen, are prime. The explanation is that a predator whose own numbers peak every two, three or four years can coincide with a thirteen-year brood only rarely, and that broods on shorter non-prime cycles would be eaten out. The main idea is that claim about primes keeping predators out of step, not any of the supporting details.

whyWrong.A: This reverses the argument; the text's point is precisely that predator peaks cannot line up with a thirteen-year cycle.
whyWrong.B: Hybrid broods on shorter non-prime cycles are described as worse off, since they can be matched by predators more often.
whyWrong.D: The text explains the mass emergence by predator satiation, numbers no predator can eat through, and never mentions food availability.

whyCorrect: The passage sets two systems side by side: harbour territories that appear on no chart and are enforced by the fishers themselves through cut warps, and a state that licenses anyone qualified and recognises none of those boundaries. The last sentence supplies the payoff, that catches per trap run higher inside the tightly held territories than along coasts where the custom has lapsed. A main idea has to join the informal system to that result, which is what this choice does.

whyWrong.B: The text says the opposite: state licensing ignores the boundaries, and the harbours go on enforcing them anyway.
whyWrong.C: Cutting warps is mentioned as the method of enforcement, not ranked against other causes of gear loss.
whyWrong.D: The comparison is between places, territories versus coasts where custom broke down, not between years, and no overall decline is claimed.

whyCorrect: Nyman is not arguing that the old vowels are weakening, which both sides accept; he is arguing about the cause, daily contact with city speech rather than decay on its own. Useful support therefore has to separate those two explanations. Tying vowel strength to how much an individual is exposed to the city, strongest in residents who never go and weakest in daily commuters, is a pattern contact predicts and self-contained fading does not.

whyWrong.A: This supports the rival explanation: if the same vowels weaken just as fast without any rail link, contact cannot be what is driving the change.
whyWrong.B: What residents say they value is an attitude, and attitudes bear on neither the rate nor the cause of the change.
whyWrong.D: Population growth is compatible with either explanation and says nothing about whether the newcomers or commuters brought city speech into daily contact.

whyCorrect: Ruiz's claim is about a specific workshop, so the evidence has to be something shared with that master's documented frescoes and not with every painter in the region. Laying the plaster in daily sections of the same size and order, and pricking the cartoons at the same spacing, are habits of working procedure that a single shop repeats from job to job. That is why this finding narrows the field to one workshop instead of merely placing the fragment in the right area.

whyWrong.A: A backlog of commissions gives the workshop a reason to produce more paintings but attaches this particular fragment to no one.
whyWrong.C: A subject painted throughout the region in that period is exactly what fails to distinguish one workshop from another.
whyWrong.D: Sand from a riverbed used across the whole province is shared by every workshop there, so it cannot single out this master.

tips: For an attribution claim, ask whether the evidence would also be true of the master's rivals; if it would, it is not support.

whyCorrect: Halloran's proposal names a specific mechanism, that the squirrel removes the particles ice would grow around. The finding that supports it has to test those particles directly. Blood from a hibernating squirrel freezing at a markedly lower temperature until fine particles are stirred in, after which it freezes more readily, shows both that the particles are what start crystals and that hibernating blood is short of them.

whyWrong.A: Periodic rewarming is a real feature of hibernation, but it says nothing about what does or does not seed ice while the animal is cold.
whyWrong.B: Burrowing below the frost line would explain never getting cold enough to freeze, whereas the fact to be explained is a body temperature already below freezing without ice forming.
whyWrong.C: Identical salts at identical concentrations rules out one alternative explanation but offers no positive evidence about particles.

whyCorrect: Follow the chain the passage builds: unfired clay crumbles in damp ground and can dissolve back into mud, the palace fire was hot enough to bake the tablets, and tens of thousands came out of the ash unbroken and legible. The word Paradoxically signals that the ending must run against what destruction normally does. The fire that ended the library is the same fire that fired the clay and made it survivable.

whyWrong.A: This contradicts the passage, which says tens of thousands of tablets were dug out in the nineteenth century.
whyWrong.B: It reverses the causation: the tablets were unfired on the shelves, and the sack is what baked them.
whyWrong.C: The text states that a great many were still legible, so unreadable is the opposite of the stated outcome.

whyCorrect: Two facts do the work here. Ants carry these seeds only as far as the nest, so the plants advance a few metres a year, and the woods in question were cleared and replanted within the last century. At that rate a hundred years buys a few hundred metres at most, which is not far enough to recolonise a replanted wood. The stem also tells you the soil is otherwise suitable, which points the explanation at time rather than at conditions.

whyWrong.B: Nothing suggests ants sort seeds by the age of the wood the parent plant grew in; the ants respond to the oil body.
whyWrong.C: Requiring soil never ploughed is a soil-quality explanation, and the stem has already told you the soil is otherwise suitable.
whyWrong.D: Shrinking oil bodies in replanted woods is a mechanism the passage never mentions and gives no basis to assume.

whyCorrect: Start by testing what stands on each side of the blank. Because the fields lie lower than the water on the far side of the bund is a subordinate clause, and a failure of the pumps lasting even a few days will drown a crop is the main clause. An introductory subordinate clause is joined to the main clause with a comma, so the comma is the only punctuation that fits.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon has to sit between two independent clauses, and the material before it begins with Because, so it cannot stand alone.
whyWrong.B: A colon also requires a complete sentence in front of it, and the Because clause is not one.
whyWrong.C: And coordinates two elements of the same kind; here it welds a subordinate clause to a main clause with no punctuation, leaving a sentence with no properly attached main statement.

tips: Cover the blank and ask whether the words before it could stand alone as a sentence; if they cannot, semicolons and colons are both out.

whyCorrect: What follows the blank is most of which have lain where they fell for tens of thousands of years, a relative clause. A relative clause is not a sentence and has to stay attached to the noun it modifies, here the stones brought back in a season. The only punctuation on offer that keeps it attached rather than cutting it loose is the comma.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides, and a clause opening with most of which cannot stand alone.
whyWrong.B: A colon introduces an explanation, a list or an appositive; a relative clause beginning with which is none of those and still needs its noun.
whyWrong.C: A period turns the relative clause into a sentence fragment with no main verb of its own to govern it.

whyCorrect: Test both halves separately. Craftsmen taken prisoner at Talas in 751 are said to have set up the first mills in Samarkand is a complete sentence, and within fifty years paper was being made in Baghdad is another. Two complete sentences with no coordinating conjunction between them need a semicolon.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation at all the two sentences fuse into a run-on.
whyWrong.B: A colon is not followed by a coordinating conjunction, and the second clause continues the chronology rather than explaining Samarkand.
whyWrong.D: A comma alone between two complete sentences is a comma splice.

whyCorrect: Both halves are complete sentences: the paint throws back almost all of the sunlight that strikes it, and it radiates the heat it does absorb at a wavelength that passes out through the atmosphere. When a coordinating conjunction such as and joins two complete sentences, a comma goes before the conjunction. That is what this choice supplies.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon already does the work of joining two sentences, so following it with and is doubling up on the join.
whyWrong.B: A colon introduces an explanation or a list, and it is never followed by a coordinating conjunction.
whyWrong.D: Dropping the comma before and leaves two independent clauses run together with nothing marking the boundary.

whyCorrect: The names belong to the men the lamps were issued to, and there are three hundred lamps, one man each, so the possessor is plural. The plural of miner is miners, and a plural noun already ending in s takes only an apostrophe after the s. That gives miners'.

whyWrong.A: Miners's is not a form English uses; a plural already ending in s never adds a second s after the apostrophe.
whyWrong.C: Miner's is the singular possessive, which would say all the names belonged to one man.
whyWrong.D: Miners with no apostrophe is a plain plural noun and shows no possession, so it cannot modify names this way.

whyCorrect: The comparison is between the panels fired in the rebuilt kiln and the panels fired in the old one, so the pronoun stands in for a plural noun, panels. Those is the plural demonstrative and can take the modifier fired in the old one after it. Read the sentence back with panels restored and only those fits.

whyWrong.B: That is singular, so it disagrees in number with the plural panels it replaces.
whyWrong.C: Them is an object pronoun and cannot head a noun phrase that is being compared and then modified by fired in the old one.
whyWrong.D: It is singular and has no plural antecedent in the sentence to refer to.

whyCorrect: Recommended that is one of the verbs that force the subjunctive in the clause after it, alongside require, insist, demand and propose. In that clause the verb appears in its base form regardless of tense or subject, so it is not be moved rather than any tensed form. Compare the familiar pattern: the doctor recommended that he rest, not that he rests.

whyWrong.A: Was not moved is a past indicative, which reports what happened instead of stating what the conservators asked for.
whyWrong.B: Will not be predicts the future; the subjunctive clause takes the base form be, not a modal.
whyWrong.D: Is not is present indicative and states a fact, which the clause after recommended that cannot do.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank lists advantages of rammed earth: no firing, no cement, almost no transport. The sentence after the blank gives another advantage, that the walls hold heat through the day and release it after dark. Since both sentences point the same way, the transition has to add rather than contrast, which is what In addition does.

whyWrong.A: Nonetheless signals that what follows runs against what came before, but a further benefit does not oppose the benefits already listed.
whyWrong.B: Otherwise introduces what would happen under the opposite condition, and no alternative condition is described.
whyWrong.C: By contrast sets two things against each other, while the thermal behaviour belongs to the same walls already being praised.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says a Chinese character gives almost no guide to pronunciation but does carry meaning, which is why speakers of mutually unintelligible dialects can read the same page. The second says an alphabetic spelling records the sound and leaves the meaning to be worked out. The two writing systems are being set against each other on exactly the same two dimensions, sound and meaning, so the transition has to mark opposition.

whyWrong.B: Accordingly claims the second statement follows as a consequence of the first, but how alphabets work is not caused by how Chinese characters work.
whyWrong.C: Similarly says the two cases match, and here they are opposites on both points.
whyWrong.D: In fact strengthens or corrects a point just made about the same subject; this sentence switches to a different writing system.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences are the premises. Type was redistributed after each run, so a reset book almost never repeats the same errors, and yet every surviving copy of the 1543 edition carries the identical misprint in the identical place. The last sentence draws the conclusion those premises force, that all the copies came from one setting of the type, so the transition has to signal a conclusion.

whyWrong.A: Meanwhile marks two things happening at the same time, and no second timeline is in play.
whyWrong.C: Nevertheless would mean the conclusion holds despite the evidence, when in fact it follows straight from it.
whyWrong.D: For example would make the last sentence an instance of the previous one, but it is an inference drawn from it.

whyCorrect: The goal fixes what counts as relevant: the student wants to explain why the drilling stopped short of its target. Only two notes give a reason, the unexpected heat at depth and the plastic rock closing the hole on the drill, and this choice uses both. The others report facts from the notes without connecting any of them to the stopping.

whyWrong.A: Start and end dates say when the project ended, not what defeated it.
whyWrong.C: How far through the crust the hole reached measures the shortfall rather than explaining it.
whyWrong.D: A depth record is a result of the drilling, and nothing in it accounts for the abandonment.

tips: On these note questions, read the stated goal first and reject any choice that is accurate but answers a different question.

whyCorrect: The stated goal is to explain why the hand calculation was done. The note that supplies a reason is that Glenn would not fly until Johnson had checked the machine's numbers herself, and this choice puts that reason in a because clause and then reports what she did. That is the only option that links cause to action.

whyWrong.A: Her years at Langley are background and give no reason for this particular calculation.
whyWrong.C: That NASA had moved to electronic computers sets the scene but does not say why anyone rechecked the output by hand.
whyWrong.D: This states what she did and with what tool, leaving out the demand that made it necessary.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why returning the oysters should improve the harbour's water, so the answer needs the mechanism, not the history. The filtering rate of a single oyster, as much as 190 litres a day, is the mechanism, and the number of oysters returned is the scale it operates at. This choice is the only one that joins those two notes into an explanation.

whyWrong.A: The number returned is half the argument, but without the filtering rate it says nothing about water quality.
whyWrong.B: The historic extent of the reefs and their destruction explain what was lost, not what the new oysters will do.
whyWrong.D: The causes of the reefs' destruction belong to the past and bear on the harbour's condition, not on the effect of restoration.

whyCorrect: The colon means what follows is evidence for the blank, and what follows is that anyone standing in the room could see for herself why the moon went dark. The set-up backs that up: a lamp, a mirror and a garden globe are physical objects arranged where the audience can watch them. A demonstration that replaces mathematics with things you can look at is a concrete one.

whyWrong.A: Abstract is the opposite; the whole point is that Wang Zhenyi built something visible for readers who had none of the mathematics.
whyWrong.B: Provisional means tentative or temporary, and nothing suggests the demonstration was a stopgap or open to revision.
whyWrong.C: Elaborate describes complexity of construction, but a lamp, a mirror and a globe are simple, and complexity would not explain why anyone in the room could follow it.

whyCorrect: The colon again gives the evidence: outside a couple of African burrowers the arrangement is found only in insects. That means almost no mammal does this, so the blank has to say rare in the extreme. Nearly unique is the hedge the sentence needs, since a couple of other burrowers keep it from being strictly one of a kind.

whyWrong.B: Universal would mean every mammal lives this way, the reverse of what the evidence after the colon says.
whyWrong.C: Obsolete describes something that has fallen out of use, but the colonies described are alive and functioning now.
whyWrong.D: Incidental means minor or beside the point, which does not fit an arrangement that organises the entire colony.

whyCorrect: Work out what the angle of the head does before you look at the options. Tipped one way the fixed carving reads as grief, tipped back it reads as composure, and nothing on the wood has moved. So the angle changes how the mask is taken, and the critics' point is that the carving alone never settles what the audience sees. Modify is the sense that matches, since qualify here means to alter or shade the effect.

whyWrong.A: Certify means to vouch for something as genuine, which has nothing to do with changing how a mask reads.
whyWrong.C: Restrict is the narrowing sense of qualify, but the angle widens the mask's range of expression rather than limiting it.
whyWrong.D: Describe would make the head angle a commentary on the mask, when the text says it changes what viewers perceive.

whyCorrect: The passage explains where the panel's strength comes from: wood is strong along the grain and weak across it, and turning each layer across the one below evens out the two directions. That is a fact about how the boards are laid up, not about the boards themselves. The contrast with the species of tree at the end of the sentence confirms that the blank must name the layering.

whyWrong.B: Thickness is never mentioned, and the explanation given turns entirely on the crossed direction of the grain.
whyWrong.C: Finish refers to a surface treatment, which plays no part in how the panel carries load.
whyWrong.D: Origin restates the idea the sentence rejects, since where the wood came from is bound up with the species being ruled out.

whyCorrect: The sentence puts two things in tension: the finished piece sounds effortless, and behind it lie days of measuring, cutting and splicing tape for every note. The blank names the relation between the sound and that labour, and it has to be one of concealment or contradiction. Belies is the precise word for an appearance that gives a false impression of what lies underneath.

whyWrong.A: Justifies would mean the effortless sound makes the labour worthwhile, which is a judgement the sentence never makes.
whyWrong.C: Records is the reverse: an effortless sound hides the work rather than preserving evidence of it.
whyWrong.D: Prolongs would mean the sound extends the labour in time, which makes no sense once the piece is finished.

whyCorrect: Read the sentence after the underlined one and notice the word therefore. Because a lorry twenty kilometres away moves the mirrors more than a real signal does, the sites record hundreds of local vibration channels and accept an event only when both sites see it within light-travel time. The underlined sentence is the difficulty that arrangement exists to answer.

whyWrong.A: No two measuring methods are set against each other; the lorry is a source of noise, not a technique.
whyWrong.B: How gravitational waves are generated is never discussed; the text is about detecting them.
whyWrong.D: The sentence says local disturbances are larger than the signal, not that no genuine signal has ever been recorded.

whyCorrect: The sentences around it describe the procedure: the assembly votes on whether to hold an ostracism, and two months later citizens scratch a name on a sherd. The underlined sentence supplies the consequence of that vote, ten years out of Attica but with property and citizenship intact. It tells you what the penalty actually was, which the description of the voting alone leaves open.

whyWrong.B: How the sherds came to be in the wells is never explained; the wells appear in the next sentence only as where they were found.
whyWrong.C: The evidence of manipulation is the bundles of sherds in one handwriting, which comes later and is not what this sentence reports.
whyWrong.D: The sentence describes the effect of one procedure on one man, not the assembly's powers in general.

whyCorrect: The question asks specifically about the pottery sequence, so the trade goods are a distraction. The finding is that the pottery below the walls is continuous with the pottery above them, meaning the same local tradition was in use before, during and after the building. If foreigners had come in and built the walls, you would expect a break in the sequence at that level. Continuity therefore points to the community already on the site as the builders.

whyWrong.A: Persian glass shows trade reaching the site, but it is not part of the pottery sequence and unbroken local pottery argues against outside builders.
whyWrong.B: Nothing in the text concerns abandonment, and continuous pottery above the walls indicates the site went on being occupied.
whyWrong.C: The text gives no stratigraphic position for the celadon, so the sequence cannot establish when it arrived relative to the walls.

tips: When the stem names one piece of evidence, answer from that evidence alone even when the passage offers others.

whyCorrect: Count the hands the passage puts on one print: the artist draws, the block cutter destroys the drawing and cuts the ridges that survive as lines, the printers pull one impression per colour and register the sheet with notches, and the publisher pays and picks the subject. The opening detail, that only the artist signs it, sets up the gap the rest of the text fills. The main idea is that a print attributed to one name is the work of a whole trade.

whyWrong.A: The registration notches are one detail in one step, and the text never ranks them against anything.
whyWrong.B: This contradicts the last sentence, which says publishers chose the subjects.
whyWrong.D: No comparison of skill between cutters and artists is made; the point is division of labour, not ranking.

whyCorrect: Tesfaye's argument has two parts, that the long interval keeps seed-eaters from building a population and that the quantity released at once swamps whatever animals are present. The finding that tests both is a comparison with stands that flower a little every year. If rodent numbers still climb in a mast year yet a far smaller proportion of the seed is eaten than in the annually flowering stands, both the scarcity of predators over time and the swamping effect are doing the work she claims.

whyWrong.B: Altitude is a fact about where the stands grow and bears on neither predator populations nor seed survival.
whyWrong.C: How fast seedlings grow in shade concerns conditions after germination, not defence against seed eaters.
whyWrong.D: Alternative foods would help rodents persist between flowerings, which works against the first half of her argument rather than supporting it.

whyCorrect: Braga's claim is that the soldiers brought their own foodways, not that the pots were shipped in. Clay dug within a few kilometres of the fort rules out import, so somebody at the fort was making pots locally, and a shape recorded only in the Rhineland says that somebody carried a Rhenish habit north with them. Those two facts together are exactly what her claim predicts.

whyWrong.A: If the same shape turns up across the empire, including North Africa, it is no longer a marker of the Rhine and points away from her claim.
whyWrong.B: The length of an emperor's reign dates the fort but says nothing about where its garrison was raised.
whyWrong.D: How common the pots are in the rubbish shows they were used heavily, not who introduced the shape.

whyCorrect: Molina is arguing against kinship as the whole explanation, so the useful evidence has to hold kinship out of the picture and still find structure in the sharing. Unrelated bats, so no kin effect, and donation to a given partner tracking how often that partner fed the donor before, which is reciprocity between particular individuals. That is her claim tested directly.

whyWrong.B: Roosting proximity is compatible with either explanation, since relatives also roost together, so it fails to separate them.
whyWrong.C: Mothers feeding their own pups is the kinship account she is arguing beyond, so it supports the alternative.
whyWrong.D: The sixty-hour limit explains why a missed meal is serious, not what keeps donors donating.

whyCorrect: Sort the sodium cell's traits into costs and benefits. The cost is energy density, since a larger, heavier ion means less energy stored per kilogram. The benefits are price per kilowatt-hour, tolerance of full discharge, and abundance. A technology that is cheap but heavy belongs wherever weight is not the binding constraint, which is what this choice says.

whyWrong.A: This inverts a stated advantage: sodium cells tolerate being run flat, so uses that discharge fully are where they do well.
whyWrong.B: Where lithium is locally abundant, the reason for reaching for sodium in the first place disappears.
whyWrong.D: Minimum weight is precisely the requirement sodium cells fail, since a sodium ion is larger and heavier than a lithium one.

whyCorrect: The stated rule is that a clock runs more slowly the deeper it sits in the gravitational field, so the size of the difference depends on the height between the two clocks. At thirty centimetres the raised clock already ran measurably ahead. Raising it to a full metre increases the separation, so the gap that opens must be larger, not smaller.

whyWrong.B: A reversal would require the lower clock to run faster, which contradicts the rule that depth slows a clock.
whyWrong.C: An unchanged gap would mean height makes no difference, but height is the very thing the effect depends on.
whyWrong.D: The gap disappears only if the two clocks sit at the same depth, and a metre of separation is more, not less.

whyCorrect: The subject of the sentence is Ibn al-Haytham, and the verb is argued. Between them sits a long non-essential description, the scholar who wrote the Book of Optics while under house arrest in Cairo, which is already opened by a comma after his name. A pair of commas has to close as well as open, so the second comma goes after Cairo.

whyWrong.A: With no comma after Cairo the interrupting description is opened but never closed, so the reader runs the modifier straight into the verb.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon must join two complete sentences, and here it would fall between the subject and its own verb.
whyWrong.D: A colon needs a complete statement in front of it, and cutting the sentence off before argued leaves none.

whyCorrect: The warehouse at Bergen dealt in almost nothing else is a complete sentence, and what follows the blank is a list of the goods it did handle: dried cod, grain and salt. A colon is the mark that introduces a list after a complete statement, and here the list spells out what almost nothing else amounts to.

whyWrong.A: And makes the cod, grain and salt additional to nothing else, which contradicts itself; the list is meant to specify that phrase, not add to it.
whyWrong.B: With no punctuation the list runs straight into else, leaving the reader no signal that a specification is starting.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon requires a complete sentence on each side, and a list of three goods is not a sentence.

whyCorrect: When the tide runs out across the sand is a subordinate clause, since When leaves it unable to stand alone, and the causeway is dry for six hours and the island stops being an island is the main clause. An introductory subordinate clause is separated from the main clause by a comma.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon needs a full sentence before it, and a clause beginning with When is not one.
whyWrong.C: A colon likewise requires a complete statement in front of it.
whyWrong.D: And coordinates equal elements, so putting it here ties a subordinate clause to a main clause and leaves the sentence without a properly introduced main statement.

whyCorrect: Although nobody who made these charts had a means of fixing longitude at sea is a subordinate clause, and the outlines of the Mediterranean on the earliest of them are accurate to within a few kilometres is the main clause. That is the standard concessive pattern, and it takes a comma at the join.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, but the Although clause cannot stand on its own.
whyWrong.B: A colon also needs a complete sentence before it, which the Although clause is not.
whyWrong.C: And would coordinate the two clauses as equals, but Although has already made the first one subordinate, so the sentence loses its footing.

whyCorrect: The grant pays for a list of three things, and the first two are already fixed in form: cataloguing the negatives and digitising the most fragile among them. Items in a list have to take the same grammatical shape, so the third must be another -ing phrase. Making the entire collection searchable online matches.

whyWrong.A: An infinitive breaks the pattern, giving cataloguing, digitising and then to make.
whyWrong.B: For the searching of adds a preposition the other two items do not have and turns the verb into an awkward noun phrase.
whyWrong.D: This is a full clause with its own subject and verb, which cannot sit in a list beside two -ing phrases.

whyCorrect: By the time the ash cloud reached the camp fixes a moment in the past, and the packing has to be finished before that moment. The tense for an action completed before a past reference point is the past perfect, had packed. The sentence then carries on with and started inland, the events that follow in sequence.

whyWrong.B: Simple past puts the packing at the same time as the cloud's arrival and loses the ordering that by the time sets up.
whyWrong.C: Have packed is present perfect, which ties the action to now and clashes with the past-time frame of that evening.
whyWrong.D: Were packing describes the action still in progress, contradicting by the time, which requires it to be done.

whyCorrect: Find the subject before the interrupting phrase: it is the collection of Persian bindings, which is singular. Together with several hundred loose folios is a parenthetical addition set off by commas, and phrases like together with, along with and as well as never change the number of the subject. Last winter fixes the tense as past, so the verb is was.

whyWrong.A: Were takes its number from folios inside the interrupting phrase rather than from the subject collection.
whyWrong.B: Are is both plural and present, and the sentence is about something finished last winter.
whyWrong.C: Have been is plural and present perfect, which conflicts both with the singular subject and with the completed past time.

commonMistakes: Letting the noun nearest the verb set the agreement when it sits inside a phrase set off by commas.

whyCorrect: The first sentence lists what ultrasonic welding does well: it joins parts in a fraction of a second and needs no adhesive. The second names a limitation, that the parts must be pressed against a fixed anvil, which rules the method out for most repairs. Advantage followed by drawback calls for a transition that marks the turn.

whyWrong.A: Likewise says the second statement matches the first, but a limitation is not another advantage.
whyWrong.B: Therefore makes the restriction a consequence of the speed and the lack of adhesive, and nothing in the first sentence causes it.
whyWrong.C: For example would make the second sentence an instance of the first, when it introduces a different kind of point altogether.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives a cause: for two hundred years the quarry sent out millstones weighing close to a tonne, each rolled on its edge down to the river. The second gives the effect, roads metalled centuries before any others in the district. A load like that on a soft road is exactly why those roads would be surfaced first, so the transition must mark a result.

whyWrong.B: Nevertheless would signal that the roads were surfaced despite the heavy traffic, when the traffic is the reason.
whyWrong.C: Meanwhile places two facts side by side in time and drops the causal link the sentences depend on.
whyWrong.D: In contrast sets the two statements against each other, but they agree.

whyCorrect: The first sentence makes a general claim, that some fish change sex and the direction varies by species. The second describes one species in detail: a clownfish group loses its breeding female and the largest male turns female to replace her. A specific case offered to illustrate a general claim takes an exemplifying transition.

whyWrong.A: In addition would make the clownfish a second separate point rather than an instance of the first.
whyWrong.C: Instead corrects or replaces what came before, but the clownfish case supports it.
whyWrong.D: As a result treats the clownfish behaviour as caused by the general statement, when the general statement is simply a summary of cases like it.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain what makes the network efficient, so the answer needs the thing that is saved. The notes give it in the first two lines: power stations throw away most of the heat they make, and Copenhagen pipes that heat to buildings instead of releasing it. Using an output that would otherwise be wasted is the efficiency, and only this choice states it.

whyWrong.B: The loop is described but never tied to any saving, so as written it reports plumbing rather than explaining efficiency.
whyWrong.C: That power stations produce a lot of heat is half the setup and says nothing about the network at all.
whyWrong.D: The 98 percent figure measures how widely the network reaches, which is coverage rather than efficiency.

whyCorrect: The stated goal is how a particular pitch is produced. Two notes bear on that: the surface is sunk into a bowl and divided into note areas by hammering, and each area is worked thinner or thicker until it sounds the pitch the tuner wants. This choice uses both, which is what turns a description of the instrument into an explanation of pitch.

whyWrong.A: Biscuit tins and brake drums are part of the instrument's history and say nothing about tuning.
whyWrong.B: What the pan is made from does not explain how one area comes to sound a given note.
whyWrong.C: The date and place of development are background, not mechanism.

whyCorrect: The goal has two halves, cutting the weight and keeping the beam, so the answer has to address both. The note that keeps the beam is that each ring bends light through the same angle as the corresponding part of a solid lens would; the note that cuts the weight is that the glass between the rings, which only added weight, was left out. This choice puts them in a because clause and its result, which is the explanation asked for.

whyWrong.B: Why the lens must be large states the constraint the design works under, not how the design met it.
whyWrong.C: That a solid lens would be too heavy to turn is the problem, and the goal asks for the solution.
whyWrong.D: Naming the innovation and its date says what was done without saying why the beam survived the loss of glass.

whyCorrect: The sentence is built as _____ enough that the animal can spend an entire life in water that would freeze other fish. The blank therefore has to name a quality that would license a whole lifetime of protection. The passage stresses that the proteins hold new crystals in check continuously rather than dissolving them, so the protection works all the time, which is what dependable captures.

whyWrong.B: Temporary contradicts an entire life in that water; a protection that lapsed would not do.
whyWrong.C: Novel describes how unusual the mechanism is, which gives no reason the fish can survive continuous cold.
whyWrong.D: Modest understates the effect and does not fit an enough that clause reporting a complete success.

whyCorrect: The sentence sets up a contrast: the figure is not applied to the surface but _____ in the metal itself. The reason is given just before it, that the bands come from carbides gathering in rows as the ingot cools, so the pattern forms as part of the metal's own structure. Inherent is the word for a property belonging to the material rather than added to it.

whyWrong.A: Concealed is wrong because the bands are plainly visible; that is what makes the blades recognisable.
whyWrong.B: Etched is surface work with acid, which is the applied treatment the sentence rules out and precisely what the later smiths did.
whyWrong.D: Imitated describes the nineteenth-century copies, not the original structure being described here.

whyCorrect: The colon supplies the evidence: the hunters carry off the honey, and the birds get the wax and grubs they could not reach on their own. Each side takes something the other cannot use or cannot obtain alone, so the blank has to name a two-way benefit. Reciprocal is that word.

whyWrong.A: One-sided is contradicted by the colon, which lists a payoff for both parties.
whyWrong.B: Recent is not supported and runs against the detail that the call is learned from fathers, implying a long-standing practice.
whyWrong.D: Accidental cannot fit an exchange in which the birds respond to one learned call and not to others.

whyCorrect: The clause before the blank tells you what to look for: the claw never touches the prey, and the phrase after it says the weapon is delivered entirely through the water. What does the damage is the collapsing vapour bubble, not contact. A weapon that reaches its target through an intervening medium rather than by touch is an indirect one.

whyWrong.A: Audible is true of the snap but answers a different question; the sentence is about how the blow reaches the fish, not about what can be heard.
whyWrong.B: Defensive misstates the use, since the passage describes stunning prey.
whyWrong.C: Reusable is never in question; nothing suggests the claw is spent after one snap.

whyCorrect: The assumed order was agriculture first, monuments afterwards, because only settled farmers could feed a workforce. Gobekli Tepe has monumental pillars raised by people with no fields at all, and the sentence itself says the site puts the building first and the farming afterwards. Swapping the two terms of an assumed sequence is what reverses means.

whyWrong.A: Postpones would mean the order happens later than expected, but the order itself is unchanged, which is not what the sentence describes.
whyWrong.C: Confirms is the opposite; the site contradicts the assumption.
whyWrong.D: Obscures would mean the order becomes unclear, whereas the site makes a definite opposite claim about which came first.

whyCorrect: Take the text one move at a time. It first describes how the Arsenal worked, hulls floated past a line of sheds each handing over one thing. Then it gives the result that shows the method's speed, a galley fitted out between morning and evening. Then it closes on what nobody did with it, since the method was never written down as a system and visitors treated it as a curiosity of Venice. That three-part shape is the structure.

whyWrong.A: No later assembly line appears in the text, and no judgement of inferiority is made.
whyWrong.C: Nothing about decline is described; the sixteenth-century visitors are cited for how they interpreted the method, not for its end.
whyWrong.D: Only one account of the fitting-out is given, so there are no competing versions to contrast.

whyCorrect: The text does three things in order: it explains the practice, districts meeting each year and delegates whose ranking bound the council; it reports a measurable outcome, a sharp rise in water and sewer spending in the poorest districts; and it grants the drawbacks, slowness and low turnout, before noting that other cities copied it. A purpose statement has to cover all three moves rather than any single one.

whyWrong.B: The council is described as bound by the ranking, not as something to be done away with; no such argument is made.
whyWrong.C: No other city's finances are examined; other municipalities appear only as imitators.
whyWrong.D: How delegates are elected is mentioned in a single clause and is not what the text is for.

whyCorrect: The passage describes cells at the wound giving up their identity, gathering into a blastema, and then being told what to become by signals from the surrounding tissue. The key detail is that those signals carry position: a blastema at the wrist makes a hand, one at the shoulder makes the whole arm. The last sentence rules out the alternative explicitly by saying nothing is copied from the lost limb, so location, not memory of what was there, decides the outcome.

whyWrong.A: This reverses the text, which makes the surrounding tissue's signals the instructing force.
whyWrong.C: No other vertebrate is mentioned and no rate of regrowth is given, so a speed claim has no basis here.
whyWrong.D: The passage says the cells give up their identity before forming the blastema, which is the opposite of retaining it.

whyCorrect: The question asks only about the return migration, so go to the sentence that describes it. Before setting out, the gut shrinks, the eyes enlarge and the body turns silver, and the eel then crosses the ocean without eating. Those are the two things the text states, a physical change beforehand and no feeding on the way.

whyWrong.A: The text says none of the tagged eels has ever returned, and the freshwater years come before the crossing, not after it.
whyWrong.C: This contradicts the passage directly, which says the animal swims back without eating and shrinks its gut first.
whyWrong.D: The first sentence says no one has ever seen a European eel spawn in the Sargasso Sea.

whyCorrect: The second account says the figures were moved standing up, rocked side to side by teams pulling on ropes. What would make that possible is a base shaped to rock rather than tip over, and figures abandoned on the transport routes are the ones caught mid-journey. A convex, forward-leaning base on exactly those figures is physical evidence for the walking method.

whyWrong.A: Plentiful timber removes the objection to the sledge-and-roller account, so it supports the first account instead.
whyWrong.B: Unfinished figures still attached to the bedrock tell you about carving in the quarry, not about how finished figures travelled.
whyWrong.C: Flat, level bases belong to figures already standing on their platforms, where stability is what you would want whichever method brought them there.

whyCorrect: Okafor's claim is about mechanism: the jump in participation came from removing effort, not from persuading people that saving is worthwhile. Evidence for it has to show that the enrolled are following the path of least resistance rather than acting on a considered judgement. Contributions bunched at the plan's default percentage rather than at the levels staff themselves called adequate show exactly that, since a persuaded saver would move the rate to what they believe they need.

whyWrong.A: Investment returns depend on markets and say nothing about why people enrolled.
whyWrong.C: General satisfaction with the employer is not evidence about the reason for a saving decision.
whyWrong.D: A rise among staff who still had to opt in would point to something other than the default, which cuts against his explanation.

whyCorrect: Ndiaye's proposal is that living bacteria on the rock surface do the concentrating, and the rival is a purely physical process of dust wetted and dried. The way to separate them is to remove the organisms and see whether enrichment still happens. Sterilised chips showing no manganese enrichment after a decade while untreated chips beside them do is that experiment, and it isolates the biological step.

whyWrong.A: Where varnish is thickest relative to the wind speaks to how dust settles, which fits the account she is arguing against.
whyWrong.B: Manganese present in settling dust supplies the rival explanation with its source rather than supporting hers.
whyWrong.C: Forming on many rock types shows only that the coating does not depend on the substrate, which both accounts already allow.

whyCorrect: The instrument works by feeling mass: a concentration of mass tugs the leading satellite forward and opens the gap. The passage then tells you groundwater is heavy and that pumping it out lightens the ground. A plain losing water month after month is losing mass month after month, so the pull it exerts on each passing satellite must get weaker over time.

whyWrong.A: The measurement described is the separation between the two satellites, and a lightening plain is precisely what changes that separation.
whyWrong.C: No change would mean the mass beneath had not altered, contradicting the steady loss of heavy groundwater.
whyWrong.D: Removing water takes mass away, so the mass measured beneath the plain falls rather than rises.

whyCorrect: Three details point the same way. The pitcher is too wide and shallow to drown anything, the rim-to-lid distance matches a shrew's length so that a feeding animal's hindquarters sit over the opening, and the fluid is rich in nitrogen of animal origin. Put together, the plant is collecting droppings from visitors it has arranged to position over the mouth, so the pitcher functions as a lavatory rather than a trap.

whyWrong.A: Rainwater would not account for nitrogen of animal origin, and it would not explain why the pitcher is shaped to a shrew's dimensions.
whyWrong.C: The nectar is bait placed under the lid to bring the shrews in, not a supply the plant keeps for itself.
whyWrong.D: Nothing about the shallow pitcher suggests a nesting site, and the shrews are described as visiting to feed.

whyCorrect: The burial held three objects nobody expected to find together is a complete sentence, and what follows names those three objects: scales, a whetstone and a coin. A colon is the mark used to introduce a list after a complete statement.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides, and a list of three objects is not one.
whyWrong.C: And placed before the first item makes the list additional to the three objects instead of identifying them.
whyWrong.D: Which introduces a relative clause and needs a verb after it, so the string of nouns that follows leaves the sentence ungrammatical.

whyCorrect: Bottle caps threaded on a wire buzz against the board as the notes sound is a complete sentence, and the tongues themselves are tuned by hammering them thinner is another. Two complete sentences with no coordinating conjunction between them are joined by a semicolon.

whyWrong.B: A comma alone between two complete sentences produces a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation, the tongues gets read as the object of sound, which changes the meaning and leaves the rest of the sentence stranded.
whyWrong.D: A colon is never followed by a coordinating conjunction, and the second clause does not explain the first.

whyCorrect: Both halves stand alone: it rose smoothly through the first two floors on the night of the dress rehearsal, and then a hydraulic seal failed and the platform sank back into the basement. Then is an adverb, not a conjunction, so it cannot join sentences by itself. That leaves the semicolon to do the joining.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation the two sentences fuse into a run-on.
whyWrong.C: A comma with only then after it is a comma splice, because then has no power to join clauses.
whyWrong.D: A colon introduces an explanation or specification, but what follows is the next event in a sequence, not an account of the first clause.

whyCorrect: The subject is Ceres and the verb is holds. Between them sits a long non-essential description, the biggest object between Mars and Jupiter and round enough to count as a dwarf planet, which is already opened by the comma after Ceres. That pair of commas has to be closed, so a comma goes after planet.

whyWrong.A: Leaving the comma out opens the interrupting description without closing it, running the modifier straight into the verb.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon must sit between two complete sentences, and here it would cut the subject off from its own verb.
whyWrong.D: A colon needs a complete statement before it, and everything before holds is only a subject with modifiers.

whyCorrect: With neither and nor, the verb agrees with whichever subject stands closer to it. Here that is the templates pinned above the bench, which is plural, so the verb is are. The rest of the passage is in the present tense as well, describing how a pan is made in general.

whyWrong.A: Was is singular and past, so it disagrees in number with templates and in tense with the surrounding description.
whyWrong.B: Has been is singular, agreeing with hammer rather than with the nearer subject templates.
whyWrong.D: Is is singular, which would be right only if the second subject were singular too.

tips: For neither A nor B, check the noun immediately before the verb, not the first one in the pair.

whyCorrect: The sentence describes storms in the decade after 1931, a finished stretch of past time, and states what those storms did. A completed action in a defined past period takes the simple past, took. The surrounding sentences use the present only for what survives today, which does not change the tense needed here.

whyWrong.A: The past perfect marks an action completed before some other past moment, but the storms come after the 1931 guidebook, so it inverts the sequence.
whyWrong.C: Take is present tense and would describe storms happening now rather than in the 1930s.
whyWrong.D: Have taken is present perfect, which does not sit with a specified and closed past period.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with the participial phrase Standing at the top of the shaft in that silence, and a phrase like that attaches to whatever noun comes first in the main clause. So the subject of the main clause must be someone capable of standing there. Only this choice supplies people, the visitors, as that subject.

whyWrong.A: This makes the pumps the thing standing at the top of the shaft, which is a dangling modifier, and the pumps are four hundred metres below.
whyWrong.B: There was the sound gives the modifier nothing human to attach to, so the phrase dangles again.
whyWrong.C: The subject is the empty it, which cannot stand anywhere, leaving the opening phrase without a doer.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says the lighthouse was automated and the keepers were taken off. The second says the fog signal went on being sounded by hand for two more winters because the timer failed in hard frost. Automation should have ended hand working, so the second sentence runs against the expectation the first creates, which calls for a concessive transition.

whyWrong.A: Because of this makes hand sounding a consequence of automation, when it is the thing automation was supposed to eliminate.
whyWrong.B: In short signals a summary, but the second sentence adds a new and contrary fact.
whyWrong.D: Likewise claims the two sentences point the same way, and they do not.

whyCorrect: The first sentence is bounded in time by Until 1861, when nearly all the cotton came from one source. The second describes a different state of affairs, buying from Egypt and India and never again depending on one harvest. The relation between them is chronological, before and after that date, so the transition has to mark what followed.

whyWrong.A: Likewise says the second situation matches the first, but it is the reverse of it.
whyWrong.B: In particular narrows to a detail of the previous statement, and this is a change of period, not a detail.
whyWrong.C: Admittedly concedes a point against the writer's own claim, and no claim is being defended here.

whyCorrect: The middle sentence states a property of the material: pulled rather than pressed, cast iron snaps with no warning. The sentence after the blank says the same thing in the terms a builder would use, that a beam cast in iron may give no sign before failing. Since it restates the preceding claim rather than adding evidence or a new case, the transition marks a rephrasing.

whyWrong.A: For example would promise an instance supporting the claim, but this sentence repeats the claim itself with no new evidence.
whyWrong.B: Earlier marks a shift back in time, and the sentence describes the same behaviour, not a previous period.
whyWrong.D: Nevertheless would set the sentence against what came before, when it agrees with it exactly.

whyCorrect: The goal is to emphasise the change of approach, so the answer has to contain both approaches and the move between them. The notes supply the abandoned method, one symbol for every word, and the method that replaced it, 85 symbols, one per syllable. This choice puts the first in a participial phrase and the second in the main clause, which is what makes the change the point of the sentence.

whyWrong.A: Rapid adoption is the outcome of the finished syllabary and says nothing about what he changed.
whyWrong.B: The span of years gives the duration of the work without naming either approach.
whyWrong.C: His own illiteracy is background about the man, not about the design decision.

whyCorrect: The goal names an apparent contradiction, individual detail alongside mass production, so the answer must hold both halves together. The note that gives mass production is the small number of moulds for the heads; the note that gives individuality is the hand modelling done afterwards. This choice joins them in a single sentence with although, which is what resolves the tension.

whyWrong.A: Paint is a finishing detail and bears on neither the moulding nor the individuality of the faces.
whyWrong.B: The circumstances of the 1974 discovery are background about the site.
whyWrong.D: The number of figures shows the scale of production but leaves the individual detailing unexplained.

whyCorrect: The goal is narrow: the effect of the 2005 dam on the northern basin. Two notes match it, the completion of the dam across the strait in 2005 and the eight-metre rise in the northern basin over the following seven months. This choice pairs the cause with the measured effect and stays inside the basin the question asks about.

whyWrong.B: The southern basin is the other side of the dam, so this reports a different effect from the one requested.
whyWrong.C: The rivers that fed the sea belong to the background before the dam existed.
whyWrong.D: The loss of volume after the 1960s diversions explains the decline the dam was built to address, not the dam's effect.

whyCorrect: The sentence contrasts two ways a language could reach the children: it was not taught to them, it was _____ by them. So the blank has to name what the children did themselves. The passage says the younger pupils produced from the pooled gestures a grammar their elders had never used, which is the creation of something new rather than the receiving of it.

whyWrong.B: Recorded would mean the children wrote down a language that already existed, but the grammar in question had never existed before.
whyWrong.C: Abandoned contradicts the passage, which describes a language coming into use and being extended by later arrivals.
whyWrong.D: Borrowed would mean taking the system from another language, yet the teachers' spoken Spanish is exactly what the pupils failed to follow.

whyCorrect: The key sentence is that most of the material is eaten on the way down. So what lands on the seabed is not a fair representation of what left the surface; it is the fraction nothing intercepted. The sentence is built as not a sample but the _____ of it, and remainder is the word for what is left after the rest has been taken.

whyWrong.A: Duplicate would make the arriving material a copy of the surface, which is the very idea the sentence rejects.
whyWrong.B: Forecast implies the deposit predicts something later, and nothing in the text points forward in time.
whyWrong.C: Measure suggests the deposit quantifies the surface reliably, but selective eating on the way down destroys that relationship.

whyCorrect: The passage says the threads are wound in the gland into a tight skein and that the gel is mostly seawater held in a mesh of those threads. To turn a thimbleful into litres in a fraction of a second, the wound skeins have to come undone and spread through the water. The sentence puts the emphasis on speed rather than quantity, so the blank names that rapid unwinding.

whyWrong.A: Dissolving would destroy the threads, but the mesh they form is what traps the water and makes the gel.
whyWrong.C: Hardening is not described anywhere; the product is a gel of seawater, not a solid.
whyWrong.D: Decay is a slow breakdown and cannot happen in a fraction of a second, nor would it produce a mesh.

whyCorrect: The passage describes a sheet whose creases run in two directions so that pulling one corner opens the whole thing in a single motion. It then says engineers want a panel the spacecraft can deploy without a separate mechanism at every hinge. The blank has to name what the creases do collectively, and the sentence before it has already set up the word: the folds together perform the job a mechanism would.

whyWrong.A: Measurement has no role here; nothing is being gauged or sized.
whyWrong.B: Obstacle reverses the point, since the pattern makes deployment easier rather than harder.
whyWrong.D: Ornament makes the creases decorative, but they are described as doing structural work.

whyCorrect: The whole passage compares two substances a painter works in, egg tempera that dries in seconds and oil that stays workable for days. The sentence with the underlined word talks about moving from one to the other and giving up a habit of working as much as a material. In that context medium means the substance the picture is made in.

whyWrong.A: The middle-position sense has no application here; nothing lies between two extremes.
whyWrong.B: The mass-communication sense belongs to newspapers and broadcasting, not to paint on a panel.
whyWrong.D: The spiritualist sense is a different word entirely and has no place in a discussion of tempera and oil.

whyCorrect: The text spends its middle in mechanism, aerials radiating fields, hands changing the capacitance, the circuit turning that into pitch and volume. It then turns to consequence: no keys, frets or stops, so nothing marks where a note lies and every pitch has to be found in empty air. The closing line joins the two, easy to sound and hard to play in tune, which is what the text is for.

whyWrong.A: No case is made for the instrument's worth or for how composers should treat it.
whyWrong.B: Theremin is named once as the inventor; nothing about his career follows.
whyWrong.C: Keys, frets and stops are mentioned only as things this instrument lacks, not as a comparison with particular instruments of the period.

whyCorrect: The sentence before it describes the equipment, a row of cameras along the track with a trip wire running from the track to each shutter. The underlined sentence tells you how that equipment produced the pictures: the horse tripped the shutters itself, in order, as it went past. It is the explanation of the method that makes the following result possible.

whyWrong.A: Nothing is conceded; the next sentence says the plates settled the question in an afternoon.
whyWrong.B: How painters had drawn the horse comes in the final clause, not here.
whyWrong.C: California appears in the preceding sentence, and this one says nothing about where the cameras stood.

whyCorrect: A main idea has to cover the whole text rather than one striking detail. Here the text gives scale, more people than London around 1100; method, some hundred and twenty mounds raised with soil carried in baskets, with no wheel and no draught animal; and end, largely empty within two centuries with no established cause. The choice that holds all three together is the right one.

whyWrong.A: The text explicitly says no single cause of the emptying has been established, so naming exhaustion of the floodplain adds a claim it refuses to make.
whyWrong.B: Nothing in the passage compares Cahokia with other settlements in North America, so only is unsupported.
whyWrong.D: Mesoamerica is never mentioned, and no borrowed plan is described.

whyCorrect: Every detail in the text is about design decisions and their reason. Consonant letters are shaped to show where the sound is made, related sounds share a shape with a stroke added, vowels are assembled from three elements, and the preface says the aim was a script an unlettered person could learn in a morning. The main idea has to join those two threads, shapes built around sounds and a structure built for learning.

whyWrong.B: The passage notes what writing Korean had meant before, but it never says Chinese characters were dropped in 1446 or at any date.
whyWrong.C: No claim is made about other writing systems, so first ever goes well beyond the text.
whyWrong.D: The vowels are described as assembled from three elements, not taken from an earlier script.

whyCorrect: Two things changed at once in these releases, the bacterium spreading and mosquito numbers falling, and Boateng says the bacterium is what cut dengue. To support him you need a case where one changed without the other. Neighbourhoods where numbers fell by the same amount with no release, and dengue did not fall, isolate the numbers as insufficient on their own.

whyWrong.A: How fast Wolbachia spreads shows the release works as intended but leaves both explanations of the dengue fall standing.
whyWrong.B: Which genus transmits dengue is background and bears on neither mechanism.
whyWrong.D: Cases falling wherever releases happened is the very result under dispute, since every release also cut mosquito numbers.

tips: When two causes move together, the useful evidence is the case where they come apart.

whyCorrect: Villalobos has to beat one specific rival explanation: that the newly visible houses and fields are simply later than the known centres, in which case they add nothing to the population living at any one time. Pottery of the same periods on the new platforms as in the long-known centres dates them to the same span. That makes the extra settlement contemporary, which is what raises the population estimate.

whyWrong.A: The height of the field walls describes how well they survive, and preservation says nothing about when they were occupied.
whyWrong.C: The efficiency of lidar explains why the features were missed before, not how many people lived there or when.
whyWrong.D: Causeways linking known centres show the centres were connected but leave the date of the new features open, which is the point in dispute.

whyCorrect: Oyelaran's claim is about timing: the carbonate marks a sudden end to the glaciation rather than ice sheets melting away separately over a long stretch. Evidence about timing is what the contact between the two rock units records. A carbonate resting straight on the glacial deposits everywhere, with no weathered surface and no gap in deposition, means almost no time passed between the ice and the carbonate anywhere in the world.

whyWrong.A: The worldwide spread of the glacial deposits is already in the passage and establishes that the glaciation was global, not that it ended quickly.
whyWrong.B: That carbonate forms in warm shallow seas explains how such rock could form after ice, without telling you how fast the change was.
whyWrong.C: Where the layer is thickest describes its distribution and leaves the speed of the transition untouched.

whyCorrect: The sentence rules out one explanation before the blank: the tubes did not close because something faster appeared on the streets, since the traffic only got worse. That leaves a change in the messages themselves. A network built to move paper canisters becomes pointless once a message can be sent as a signal instead of an object, which is what happened by the 1980s.

whyWrong.A: The time of day is irrelevant, since the passage says a canister crossed a capital in minutes at any hour.
whyWrong.B: Cost of writing is never discussed, and the tubes charged by the canister regardless.
whyWrong.C: Nothing suggests messages grew physically heavier, and letters do not.

whyCorrect: The last sentence gives you the reasoning: these houses were built by families who had built in timber elsewhere, so their preference cannot be what changed. What changed is the place, where there is no timber within a hundred miles and no money to freight any in, and where turf costs nothing but labour. So the material was chosen by what the site could supply.

whyWrong.B: No regulations are mentioned, and inventing one ignores the reason the text actually supplies.
whyWrong.C: Speed of cutting is never discussed; the passage stresses the absence of timber and money, not the pace of the work.
whyWrong.D: A taste for turf is what the final sentence rules out, since the same families had built in timber when timber was available.

whyCorrect: Everything before the blank belongs to a subordinate clause opened by Because, running from fresh horses all the way to Beijing. The main clause is a dispatch could travel at a speed no single horse and no single rider could have sustained. An introductory subordinate clause is joined to its main clause with a comma.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon demands a complete sentence on both sides, and the Because clause cannot stand alone.
whyWrong.B: A colon also needs a complete statement in front of it, which this clause is not.
whyWrong.C: And coordinates equal elements, so it cannot fasten a subordinate clause to the main clause; the result has no properly introduced main statement.

whyCorrect: The subject is Meroe and the verb is holds. Between them sits a non-essential description, the capital of the kingdom of Kush for some six hundred years, and the comma after Meroe has already opened it. Interrupting phrases take commas on both sides, so a comma has to close it after years.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon has to join two complete sentences, and here it would fall between the subject and its verb.
whyWrong.B: A colon needs a full statement before it, but everything up to years is only a subject with a modifier attached.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation the description is opened by a comma and never closed, running straight into the verb.

whyCorrect: Test each side. Bessemer found that blowing cold air up through molten pig iron burns out the carbon and raises the temperature rather than lowering it is a complete sentence, and a converter of thirty tons could be blown in twenty minutes with no fuel under it at all is another. Two complete sentences with no coordinating conjunction take a semicolon.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation the two sentences fuse, and it a converter reads as a single garbled phrase.
whyWrong.B: A colon is not followed by a coordinating conjunction, so colon plus and is not a usable join.
whyWrong.D: A comma between two complete sentences is a comma splice.

whyCorrect: The material listing the pitch, the rhythm and the length of every syllable is an interruption inserted between the subject, a phrase beaten out on the drum, and its verb, is recognisable. That interruption was opened with a dash, and a pair of interrupting marks has to match, so it must close with a dash too.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon cannot close a dash, and it would also separate the subject from its own verb.
whyWrong.B: A colon likewise cannot pair with an opening dash, and no complete statement precedes it.
whyWrong.D: A comma does not match the opening dash, so the interruption is left with mismatched punctuation on either side.

whyCorrect: The subject is Each, not beacons. Of the nine beacons on the estuary is a prepositional phrase describing that subject, and prepositional phrases never supply the noun the verb agrees with. Each is singular, so the verb is has.

whyWrong.A: Have agrees with beacons inside the of-phrase rather than with the singular subject Each.
whyWrong.C: Having is a participle, not a finite verb, so the sentence would be left with no main verb at all.
whyWrong.D: Were having is plural and puts a state of possession into the past progressive, which fits neither the subject nor the sense.

whyCorrect: What is being compared is the salinity at the mouth with the salinity at the upstream gauge, and salinity is singular. That is the singular substitute that stands in for a noun already mentioned and can take a modifier after it, giving twice that recorded at the upstream gauge.

whyWrong.B: Those is plural, but the noun it would replace, salinity, is singular.
whyWrong.C: Them is an object pronoun and cannot head the second half of a comparison.
whyWrong.D: Which introduces a relative clause and needs its own verb, so it cannot stand as the thing being compared.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with Of the three, so the eastern track is being ranked against two others, not one. English uses the superlative for a comparison among three or more, which gives shortest.

whyWrong.A: Short states a quality without any comparison, but Of the three announces one.
whyWrong.B: Shorter is the comparative form, correct only when two things are being weighed against each other.
whyWrong.D: More short is not a form English uses; a one-syllable adjective takes the -er and -est endings.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences give a problem and a response: columns of figures that the intended readers had every reason to ignore, and the same figures redrawn as wedges whose areas stand for the deaths. The sentence after the blank reports what that redrawing achieved, a reader seeing at a glance what the table would have hidden. Effect following cause calls for a resultative transition.

whyWrong.A: Nevertheless would mean the reader understood despite the diagram, when the diagram is what made it possible.
whyWrong.B: Similarly claims the third sentence matches the second, but it states the consequence of it.
whyWrong.C: In contrast sets the sentences against each other, and they run in the same direction.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank lists what a hydraulic ram is: two moving parts, no external supply, powered by the momentum of the water itself. The sentence after the blank says a ram runs unattended for years at the cost of an occasional valve. That durability follows directly from having almost nothing to break and nothing to feed it, so the link is causal.

whyWrong.B: In addition treats years of unattended running as a separate fact, when it is what the simplicity produces.
whyWrong.C: For example would make the sentence an instance of the previous claim, but it states its consequence.
whyWrong.D: By contrast belongs earlier, where the electric pump is set against the ram; the two sentences here agree.

whyCorrect: The antlion cuts its pit as steep as sand will hold so that the slope itself carries an ant down, and the trapdoor spider sinks a burrow with a hinged lid so that the ground itself hides it. Both sentences describe a predator that gets the surroundings to do the work for it. Two parallel cases making the same point take a transition of likeness.

whyWrong.A: Consequently would make the spider's burrow a result of the antlion's pit, and the two animals are unconnected.
whyWrong.C: Nevertheless signals a contrast, but the second example illustrates the same principle as the first.
whyWrong.D: For example would make the spider an instance of the antlion's behaviour rather than a separate case alongside it.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain how one voice makes two parts, so the answer needs the mechanism. Two notes carry it: the melody consists of overtones already present in the drone rather than a second note, and reshaping the mouth and tongue strengthens one overtone while damping the rest. Putting those together explains why nothing extra has to be sung.

whyWrong.A: This states the effect to be explained, that two parts are heard at once, and stops there.
whyWrong.C: The names of the styles are cultural background and bear on nothing acoustic.
whyWrong.D: Singing while riding without accompaniment describes the setting, not how the two parts are produced.

whyCorrect: The goal asks for a difficulty the programme has to work around, which means an ongoing constraint on what the programme can do. The note that supplies one is that females breed only in heavy rimu fruiting years, every two to four years, so chicks can be added only that often. This choice states the constraint and its consequence for the recovery effort.

whyWrong.A: The species description and the 1995 low point set out the emergency rather than a constraint the programme works around.
