whyWrong.C: The bare figure of 51 birds measures how bad things were, not what limits the work.
whyWrong.D: Transmitters and individual files describe how intensively the birds are managed, which is a feature of the programme, not an obstacle to it.

whyCorrect: The goal is comparability between ships, so the answer must contrast the old private wording with a shared standard and say what the standard was. The relevant notes are that captains had used whatever words they chose and that each force was defined by the sail a full-rigged ship could carry in it. This choice joins them, which is what explains why one captain's entry now meant something to another.

whyWrong.A: The state of affairs before 1805 is only the problem; on its own it explains nothing about the fix.
whyWrong.B: Thirteen numbered forces and a compulsory rule tell you a scale existed and was enforced, without saying what made the numbers mean the same thing to different ships.
whyWrong.D: Attaching speeds in the twentieth century is a later development and post-dates the comparability being explained.

whyCorrect: The blank refers back to the same property discussed throughout: each kind of phage attacks only a narrow range of hosts. That narrowness counted against phages when broad antibiotics arrived, and the same trait now counts for them because a phage leaves the patient's other bacteria alone. The word that names narrowness of target is specificity.

whyWrong.A: Delay is not a property of phages that the passage names; the difficulty described is matching a phage to a strain, not waiting.
whyWrong.B: Toxicity is never attributed to phages, and the sentence needs the trait that is both drawback and virtue.
whyWrong.C: Expense is never mentioned, and cost would not become a virtue when resistance spreads.

whyCorrect: The sentence sets materials against form: the tradition is _____ about materials while remaining exact about form. The evidence is that the palette widened when commercial paint arrived and the geometry did not change at all. So the blank has to describe a willingness to take up new materials without loosening anything else, which is flexibility.

whyWrong.B: Secretive would concern who is told about the practice, and nothing in the text is withheld.
whyWrong.C: Indifferent overshoots: the painters take up new paints deliberately and use them within an unchanged geometry, which is adaptation rather than not caring.
whyWrong.D: Exacting is the quality assigned to the form half of the contrast, so using it for materials collapses the opposition the sentence builds.

whyCorrect: The text defines the word for you inside the dash: the burden is the line sung after every stanza, which the whole room joins in. That is the technical sense of the term in song, a refrain. The surrounding contrast supports it, since the verses vary from village to village and this repeated line is what holds the versions together.

whyWrong.A: The heavy-load sense is the everyday meaning, but nothing here is being carried.
whyWrong.C: The main-point sense of burden exists but does not fit a line the room sings after each stanza.
whyWrong.D: An imposed duty is another everyday sense and has no bearing on the structure of a ballad.

whyCorrect: The screen and the removed shoes have one purpose, stated in the middle sentence: to keep the panel's attention on the sound. The blank completes made the judgement _____ of everything about a player that could be seen. What the screen achieves is a decision that owes nothing to visible information, and independent is the word that takes of and carries that sense.

whyWrong.B: Suspicious would describe an attitude of the panel toward what it sees, but the screen removes the visual information entirely.
whyWrong.C: Typical says the judgement resembles others, which the sentence is not about.
whyWrong.D: Protective points at shielding the player, whereas the sentence is about what the judgement is based on.

whyCorrect: The reason clause before the blank is that the tower has no moving parts and consumes nothing. Both of those are about what the tower costs to keep running rather than what it costs to put up. So the blank names the ongoing kind of cost that is absent, which is a recurring one.

whyWrong.A: Apparent would hint that the cost is hidden rather than absent, but the passage says the tower consumes nothing at all.
whyWrong.C: An initial cost is exactly what a masonry shaft above the roof does involve, and nothing in the reason clause denies it.
whyWrong.D: Social cost is not raised anywhere in the passage.

whyCorrect: The sentence after the underlined one works out what follows from it: a burst hose, a parted coupling, a carriage breaking loose all drop the pressure, and because pressure holds the brakes off, every one of those events stops the train. So the underlined sentence supplies the decision, and the rest of the text supplies its consequences.

whyWrong.A: Steam is never mentioned, so no preference between working fluids is being explained.
whyWrong.B: Nothing is conceded; the design choice is presented as the thing that makes the system safe.
whyWrong.D: Hand braking is described in the first sentence, and this sentence is about Westinghouse's air system instead.

whyCorrect: The underlined sentence makes the claim the passage exists to support: one root system, one set of genes, therefore one organism rather than a wood full of them. The sentence that follows develops exactly that, contrasting the hundred and fifty years of a single trunk with far older roots that keep putting up replacements. The underlined sentence is the thesis and what follows is its elaboration.

whyWrong.B: It asserts that every trunk carries the same genes; it does not put that in doubt.
whyWrong.C: Trunk lifespan appears in the next sentence, and this one gives no reason for it.
whyWrong.D: No other organism is mentioned anywhere in the text, so no comparison is being drawn.

whyCorrect: The second sentence tracks the entering female from start to finish: she forces through a passage so narrow that she loses her wings and often her antennae, lays her eggs, pollinates the flowers and dies inside. Everything the question asks about is in that one sentence. The other events in the passage belong to the next generation, which hatches after she is dead.

whyWrong.A: Chewing the exit is done by the males that hatch inside, not by the female who arrived.
whyWrong.B: The mating in the dark is done by the wasps that hatch from the eggs; the arriving female mated before she came.
whyWrong.C: It is the new females who fly off with pollen; the text says the founding female dies inside the fig.

whyCorrect: The pivot is the sentence saying the older text was not removed so much as thinned, because iron in the original ink had bitten into the skin and stayed there. That is why anything is recoverable at all. X-ray fluorescence then maps that iron without touching the page and brings most of the earlier writing back. The main idea has to join the surviving trace to the method that reads it.

whyWrong.A: The stated reason for reuse is the expense of parchment, and no attitude to mathematics is mentioned.
whyWrong.B: The technique is used to recover the erased writing, not to date the skin.
whyWrong.D: No judgement is offered about which text matters more; the interest is in reading the one underneath.

whyCorrect: Ferreira says the fungus moves carbon for itself, and the rival says trees pass it to one another deliberately. Two things separate those accounts: where the carbon ends up and whether delivery responds to a tree's need. Most of the labelled carbon staying in fungal tissue answers the first, and the small remainder arriving whether or not the second tree is short of carbon answers the second, since deliberate help would track need.

whyWrong.B: Speed of transfer tells you the link works but nothing about who is moving the carbon or why.
whyWrong.C: Better survival of seedlings near a large tree is the observation the rival account is usually built on, so it points the other way.
whyWrong.D: Linking across species describes the network's reach, which both explanations accommodate.

whyCorrect: Achebe's claim has two halves, that reputation holds the arrangement together and that enforceable penalties do not. This finding tests both at once: default is rarest where members are neighbours or fellow worshippers, which is where standing costs most to lose, and no club in the sample has ever recovered money through a court, which shows the legal penalty is not doing the work.

whyWrong.A: Scarce bank branches explain why people form such clubs, not why members keep paying after taking the pot.
whyWrong.B: Drawing lots settles who goes first and says nothing about what deters a member who has already collected.
whyWrong.D: That early takers gain more sharpens the temptation to default; it does not identify what restrains them.

whyCorrect: Solve has to show the pulses do something other than communicate, so the test must remove the audience. A fish alone in a tank has no one to signal to, and its pulse rate rises when an unfamiliar object appears and falls once it has swum round the object. That is behaviour tied to inspecting a thing, which is what using the pulses to locate objects means.

whyWrong.B: Distinguishable waveforms are what would let one fish recognise another, which is evidence for the signalling account she is arguing beyond.
whyWrong.C: A rise when two fish share a tank is also the signalling account, since the second fish is the obvious audience.
whyWrong.D: The tissue the electric organ develops from is anatomy and says nothing about what the pulses are used for.

whyCorrect: Track the silica as a budget. It comes in from rivers at a measured rate, and it goes out when diatom cases sink and are buried rather than returning to the surface. Blooms strip the surface but that is a redistribution, not a source or a sink. Over the long run the amount available at the surface is set by what those two flows leave behind.

whyWrong.A: Surface temperature is never mentioned and enters neither the supply nor the loss.
whyWrong.B: The number of species does not change how much silica arrives from rivers or how much is buried.
whyWrong.D: Where a sinking case comes to rest does not matter to the budget; what matters is whether the silica is buried or returned.

whyCorrect: The passage builds one mechanism: because sound speeds up with warmth and with pressure, there is a depth of minimum speed, and sound straying above or below it is bent back. That means a call made at that depth is trapped and travels enormously far, while the same call made elsewhere leaks away. So what decides the range is where the call is made, not how loud it is.

whyWrong.B: Surface temperature helps set where the minimum lies, but the sentence asks what the range of a given call depends on, and that is whether it is made in the channel.
whyWrong.C: The animal's size bears on loudness, which is the factor the sentence has already set aside.
whyWrong.D: Direction is never discussed; the bending described works on sound straying up or down regardless of aim.
